BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE
OF
ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS

EXCEPTIONS OF INTERVENOR JOHN BRADLEY OF LAZY S RANCH TO THE PROPOSAL
FOR DECISION
 Intervenor John Bradley of Lazy S Ranch, appearing pro se, respectfully and timely ﬁles this
Exception to the Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) pursuant to 16 Texas Administrative Code
(“TAC”) § 22.261(d). This Exception concerns the PFD’s treatment of the notice
requirements applicable to the Application and the public participation meeting, and the
signiﬁcance of the August 27, 2026 memorandum of Chairman Thomas Gleeson in Docket
No. 59315.

Mr. Bradley respectfully requests that the Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) amend or
supplement the PFD as requested below and continue to recommend denial of the
Application.

EXCEPTION 1: THE CHAIRMAN’S AUGUST 27, 2026 MEMORANDUM IN DOCKET NO.
59315 DOES NOT RESOLVE THE NOTICE VIOLATIONS FOUND IN THIS PROCEEDING

The PFD correctly recognizes that Applicants did not comply with both 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3),
governing notice of the Application, and 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4), governing the required public
participation meeting. Those are separate requirements serving di erent purposes.

Section 22.52(a)(3) concerns notice of the Application itself. That notice is directed to
persons entitled to receive direct mail notice of the Application and is associated with the
opportunity to intervene and participate after the Application and proposed routes have
been ﬁled.

Section 22.52(a)(4), by contrast, concerns the public meeting that must occur before the
ﬁling of the licensing application when the rule’s numerical threshold is met. The public
meeting serves a di erent function because it occurs while routing alternatives may still be
considered and changed.

The PFD found that Applicants violated § 22.52(a)(3). The ALJs found that Applicants relied
upon appraisal-district information beginning December 8, 2025, for notices mailed March
26, 2026, although the rule requires the applicable rolls to be current as of the ﬁling date.
The ALJs further found that more than three dozen directly a ected landowners did not
receive timely Application notice and that Craig and Carleen Edwards of Link E12 never
received Application notice despite purchasing their home in August 2025.

Those ﬁndings establish an independent notice violation. The PFD should expressly state
the legal consequence of that violation rather than ﬁnding the violation and attaching no
remedy or consequence to it.

The August 27, 2026 memorandum of Chairman Thomas Gleeson in Docket No. 59315
does not alter that conclusion. In that memorandum, the Chairman addressed the public-
 meeting question under § 22.52(a)(4). The memorandum also stated that, in Docket No.
59315, the ALJs had found that Oncor was compliant with Application notice requirements.

The circumstances here are materially di erent.

Here, the ALJs found a violation of § 22.52(a)(3). The Chairman’s reasoning concerning §
22.52(a)(4) therefore does not resolve whether Applicants complied with § 22.52(a)(3) in
this proceeding. A decision concerning one subsection of the rule should not be extended
to a separate subsection involving di erent conduct, di erent a ected landowners, and a
di erent procedural opportunity.

The PFD’s ﬁndings concerning the public-meeting violation are likewise materially di erent
from the facts addressed in the Chairman’s memorandum. After the June 2025 public
meetings, Applicants expanded the study area, added approximately 400 miles of new
route links, and brought approximately 1,400 additional landowners within the class
entitled to direct mail notice of the Application. The a ected landowner class therefore
increased from approximately 2,800 to approximately 4,200.

The PFD further found that no additional public meetings were held before the Application
was ﬁled and that landowners within the expanded study area and within 500 feet of the
centerline of the newly created links did not receive notice of a public meeting.

Those ﬁndings matter because § 22.52(a)(4) contains two distinct requirements. First,
when 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct mail notice of the Application,
the utility must hold at least one public meeting before ﬁling. Second, direct-mail notice of
that public meeting must be provided to the persons identiﬁed by the rule.

The phrase “at least one” establishes a minimum, not a permanent safe harbor for every
subsequent change to the project. The rule does not state that a meeting held before
hundreds of miles of new route links are created necessarily satisﬁes the rule as to
landowners who became a ected only afterward.

Nor does the Chairman’s memorandum answer the separate question whether the
approximately 1,400 newly a ected landowners were given the public-meeting opportunity
contemplated by § 22.52(a)(4). The PFD found that these landowners were unable to
identify routing constraints or address concerns at a public meeting, to their prejudice.

An opportunity to intervene after the Application is ﬁled is not equivalent to an opportunity
to participate in the pre-application public meeting process. By the time an Application is
ﬁled, the routes have been developed and selected to a substantially greater degree. The
public-meeting requirement exists precisely so that a ected persons may provide
information and raise routing concerns before that point.
 The PFD’s ﬁndings therefore establish two separate and mutually reinforcing notice
defects:

   1. Applicants failed to comply with § 22.52(a)(3) by failing to provide timely Application
      notice to all persons entitled to receive it, including a landowner who never received
      Application notice; and

   2. Applicants failed to comply with § 22.52(a)(4) because the project was materially
      expanded after the public meetings, approximately 1,400 additional landowners
      were brought within the a ected class, no additional public meeting was held, and
      the newly a ected landowners did not receive notice of a public meeting.

Under 16 TAC § 22.262(a)(1)(A), the Commission may change a ﬁnding of fact or conclusion
of law only upon the grounds speciﬁed by the rule, and § 22.262(b) requires the
Commission to state in writing the speciﬁc reason and legal basis for such a change. The
Commission should therefore not treat the Chairman’s memorandum in Docket No. 59315
as controlling the materially di erent notice issues established in this record without
addressing the distinctions identiﬁed above.

REQUESTED RELIEF

Intervenor John Bradley respectfully requests that the ALJs amend or supplement the
Proposal for Decision to provide that:

1. Applicants’ failure to comply with 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3), as found in the PFD,
independently supports denial of the Application;

2. Applicants’ failure to comply with 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4), including the failure to provide
the required public-meeting opportunity to the approximately 1,400 landowners brought
into the a ected class after the prior meetings, independently supports denial of the
Application or, at minimum, materially compounds the prejudice to a ected landowners;

3. The August 27, 2026 memorandum of Chairman Thomas Gleeson in PUC Docket No.
59315 does not resolve the § 22.52(a)(3) violation found in this proceeding and does not
establish compliance with § 22.52(a)(4) as to the materially expanded class of a ected
landowners in this docket;

4. The approximately 1,400 newly a ected landowners were denied the opportunity to
identify routing constraints and address concerns at a pre-application public meeting, as
found in the PFD, and that prejudice cannot be treated as cured merely by the opportunity
to intervene after the Application was ﬁled;
 5. The notice violations should be given legal e ect in the Commission’s determination
whether Applicants satisﬁed the requirements applicable to the Application; and

6. Most importantly, the ALJs should continue to recommend denial of the Application
for a Certiﬁcate of Convenience and Necessity (“CCN”), because Applicants’ failures to
comply with the mandatory notice requirements materially prejudiced a ected
landowners and prevent the Application from receiving the beneﬁt of a process that
complied with 16 TAC § 22.52.

Mr. Bradley further requests such other and further relief to which he may be entitled under
the record, PURA, and the Commission’s rules.

Respectfully submitted,

JOHN BRADLEY
Intervenor, Lazy S Ranch
Pro Se

16767 Crows Ranch Rd

Salado, TX 76571

972-849-6886

Jaybradley79@yahoo.com



Signed J B Bradley III
